articles.title: How to prepare for Norway's citizenship and social studies exams
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        One of the requirements to become a citizen in Norway is to pass either the social studies or the citizenship test. The Local has put together some advice on how to best prepare.

The process of acquiring Norwegian citizenship takes years, thanks to the residence requirements, and other conditions such as the language exams, background check, citizenship, or social studies test mean it's a far from straightforward road.

Still, it should be worth it in the end, even if you have to wait a lengthy time to receive a decision on your application due to long processing times.

The main difference between which test you may take will depend on the type of residence you were granted when you first moved to Norway.

The state offers an introduction to Norway programme to some people who move to Norway. This course, usually provided along with language training, aims to get new arrivals up to speed with the country.

Those typically offered these courses originally arrived in Norway on a family immigration or asylum seeker permit.

If you arrived in Norway under the EEA or work permit rules, then you will not have been offered this course.

For those who have done this introductory course, you will likely have been presented with the opportunity to sit the social studies exam. If you have sat and passed this exam in Norwegian, then you are all set, as the exam doesn't have an expiration date and can be submitted with the rest of your documents.

Even if you didn't get the chance to sit this exam in Norwegian or complete the course, fret not, the syllabus for the course will be the same as for the citizenship exam. Therefore, you should have picked up a few things that will be useful for the test.

Most applicants who didn't do the social studies course will probably prefer the citizenship test as it is slightly easier.

The reason it's easier isn't the content of the test itself, as both tests are drawn from the same syllabus. Instead, the language used in the citizenship test is considered more accessible.

Both tests require knowledge of Norwegian history, the school system, healthcare, politics, and geography. They also include questions on societal norms in Norway, working life, and government agencies.

The syllabus is available online and can be divided into the topics of "education skills and the labour market," "family, health and daily life," and "Norway now and before."

These different topics are broken down into various sub-topics. These topics will cover how a system works in Norway and the cultural values behind a particular system – understanding both will give you the tools you need to ace either exam.

Course materials are available in several languages (however, the online portal can be glitchy). The curriculum is found on the website of HK-dir (The Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills).

Thankfully, having the curriculum available should help.

Another helpful aspect of the online curriculum is that it includes discussion points and multiple-choice questions.

For the discussion points, ask somebody to read out the questions to you in English or Norwegian as another way of testing your retention.

There is also an official mock available online. The only downside is that the questions don't change. Still, it should be good for familiarising yourself with how your knowledge will be tested and learning the language used for the test.

There are also unofficial practise exams online. Some of these charge users for access to example questions. Still, there are free mocks available online that applicants can take.

With the right preparation, you should be able to sit the test when you feel ready rather than rushing into it. Local municipalities are responsible for providing the exams and there are quite a few opportunities to take the test throughout the year.

If you need more time to get up to speed with your Norwegian reading skills, or the syllabus then its better to wait a few weeks or couple of months for more slots to open up.

Alternatively, if you want everything ready to submit when you meet the residence requirements, and your Norwegian skills are good enough, then you can take the test ahead of time.

Either way, there's no point in booking a police appointment to hand your documents in until you've passed the test – so there shouldn't be any need to put yourself under any pressure.

articles.title: Tiltalt for frihetsberøvelse av 12-åring
articles.content:
En mann i 40-årene er tiltalt for frihetsberøvelse etter å ha holdt en 12-åring som lekte «ring på og stikk» sperret inne i fjor høst.

Ifølge politiet holdt mannen barnet fast inntil en vegg før han dro henne med seg inn inn i huset og ned i kjelleren. Mannen skal også ha uttalt «du vet at du ikke kommer hjem i natt» til jenta, skriver Avisa Oslo.

Hun ble sluppet ut etter drøyt 15 minutter, da en nabo ringte på døra.

Mannen er også tiltalt for kroppskrenkelse etter å ha løpt etter, holdt fast og dratt i et annet barn som hadde ringt på døra hans rundt en måned tidligere.

Rettssaken skal gå i Oslo tingrett i desember. Det er ikke kjent hvordan mannen stiller seg til anklagene, ifølge avisa.

Oslo politidistrikt

Oslo politidistrikt omfatter kommunene Oslo, Asker og Bærum. Politimester i Oslo siden mai 2023 er Ida Melbo Øystese.

Saker i Oslo tingrett

Oslo tingrett er Norges største tingrett og behandler straffesaker, sivile saker og forvaltningssaker. Tingretten holder til i Oslo tinghus, midt i Oslo sentrum.

articles.title: Iran: Beslagla en amerikansk undervannsdrone i Hormuzstredet
articles.content:
Den iranske revolusjonsgarden (IRGC) hevder søndag å ha beslaglagt en amerikansk undervannsdrone i Hormuzstredet.

– Gjennom en koordinert og kompleks operasjon med etterretningsovervåking og elektronisk krigføring lyktes personell fra IRGCs marinestyrke med å kapre et avansert ubemannet undervannsfartøy tilhørende den terroristiske amerikanske militærmakten, heter det i en uttalelse fra IRGCs marinestyrker, ifølge statlig iransk TV.

De mener undervannsdronen drev spionasjevirksomhet i det strategisk viktige stredet. Dronen blir nå undersøkt av IRGCs spesialister, opplyses det.

Tidligere denne måneden opplyste Revolusjonsgarden at de hadde tatt beslag i en amerikansk undervannsdrone, også den i Hormuzstredet. Da gikk USA ut og bekreftet at en av deres undervannsdroner ett døgn tidligere «sviktet» i Hormuzstredet, men kommenterte ikke opplysningen om at den havnet i Revolusjonsgardens hender.

Siden USA og Israel gikk til angrep mot Iran 28. februar 2026, har krigen herjet i landet og flere områder i Midtøsten. Iran svarte med å blant annet blokkere Hormuzstredet. Det pågår fredsforhandlinger mellom landene,

articles.content:
Saudi-Arabia advarte FNs medlemsland lørdag om at forsøk på å blokkere vannveier i Midtøsten utgjør en trussel mot den globale energisikkerheten.

Landets representant krevde at det internasjonale samfunnet gjør mer for å forsvare navigasjonsfriheten, skriver AFP.

«Det internasjonale samfunnet har forsømt sitt ansvar med å konfrontere alt som truer internasjonal fred og sikkerhet,» sa utenriksminister Faisal bin Farhan til FNs generalforsamling.

Saudi-Arabia

Saudi-Arabia er et dypt religiøst monarki i Midtøsten. Det islamske landet er ofte kritisert for at kvinner har svært innskrenkede rettigheter. Landet har enorme oljeforekomster.

De forente nasjoner (FN)

FN ble opprettet like etter andre verdenskrig, i hovedsak for å unngå lignende krigssituasjoner i framtiden. Hovedkontoret ligger i New York i USA, og organisasjonen har 193 medlemsland.

Krig og konflikt i Midtøsten

Etter angrepet mot Israel 7. oktober 2023 har situasjonen i Midtøsten stadig forverret seg. Det har vært daglige rakettangrep mellom Israel og Iran-støttede Hizbollah i Libanon. Eksperter frykter storkrig.

articles.title: Flyplass stengt etter vulkanutbrudd på Sicilia
articles.content:
På Sicilia er flyplassen midlertidig stengt som følge av et utbrudd fra vulkanen Etna.

Inn- og utgående flyoperasjoner ved Fontanarossa lufthavn er suspendert til kl. 12 i morgen, søndag 27. september.

Det skriver flyplassen i Catania på sine hjemmesider.

Etna er den mest aktive vulkanen i Europa. Flyplassen måtte også stenge 13. august på grunn av aske fra vulkanen.

Vulkanen «Etna»

Det er utbot frå den sicilianske vulkanen Etna igjen. Det er Europas mest aktive vulkan, og i desember i fjor blei det registrert 130 jordskjelv etter uvanleg høg aktivitet i vulkanen.

articles.title: 'We truly understand that anxiety': The human side of Norway’s immigration system upgrade
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norway is rebuilding its immigration system through a six-year project. But will it be different this time, and are applicants truly being put first? The Local spoke to Henrik Hansen, Product Lead for the ModUlf project, to learn more.

For years, international residents in Norway have described dealing with immigration authorities as a cold, rigid, and deeply anxious experience.

Authorities are now developing ModUlf, a massive six-year overhaul across the Directorate of Immigration (UDI), the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (UD), and the police.

It is the Norwegian state’s multi-year initiative to modernise its entire immigration infrastructure and transform the application process for the international community in Norway.

In our previous article, we covered the project's overall goals and what is currently live.

READ ALSO: Inside ModUlf: What's changing in Norway's immigration process?

But as Norway undertakes the major ModUlf project, a key question remains: Does this tech upgrade care about the human side of immigration?

The Local spoke with Henrik Hansen, Product Lead (Produktleder) for the ModUlf project, about user anxiety, potential transition delays, and why officials need input from foreign residents.

When asked whether the technical teams and engineers building these new systems truly care about the stress and anxiety that immigration delays cause applicants, Hansen gave a reassuring-sounding answer.

"I do understand why people worry. It is incredibly difficult to overcome the immigration process as an applicant, so we truly understand that anxiety. But we try to place a major focus on this," Hansen said. "In many of the meetings I am in now, when we're planning, we're always asking: 'How does this feel for the applicant? How does this affect the applicant?' We're always trying to push and think about that, because if you don't actively force yourself to think about it, it's very easy to just design systems that simply improve your own workday."

Hansen explained that in the past, the focus was mostly internal. Now, the development strategy makes teams put the applicant's experience first.

"Improving my day, or the day of a caseworker in UDI, might help a little bit, but in general, we are an organisation which is heavily applicant-focused," he said. "I think, or I hope, we are moving there, focusing more on the human side. We have a good amount of people now who are constantly pushing and making sure that we remember this.”

"It is also a fundamental part of our official mandate,” Hansen further explained. “One of the most important goals of this programme is that we are supposed to make the applicant feel secure. We're supposed to make them self-sufficient, able to do things by themselves where they can clearly understand the process, see what they need to do, and complete it without having to call us or waste hours of time. We want them to understand implicitly what the system is doing, so that's definitely the ultimate goal we are working towards," he said.

READ MORE: Inside ModUlf: How Norway is rebuilding its immigration system

Will these tech upgrades delay current applications?

Many people in the international community worry that UDI processes will take even longer with this six-year upgrade. When asked if this could cause more delays, Hansen responded with transparency.

"I can't say explicitly that delays won't happen, because it's difficult to know everything. So far it has been okay, and we try to implement things without stopping as everything needs to run at the same time in a way. Our methodology is, of course, to avoid affecting applicants as much as we possibly can,” Hansen said.

He explained that even if some applications are still handled by the old system while others use the new one, they cross-reference everything to prevent problems. “But of course it is difficult to make systems, and it might happen in the future," Hansen noted.

Managing a big digital change across the government is also a tough administrative task. Hansen pointed out that running a project with many agencies means balancing very different institutional cultures and ways of working.

“One of our main goals is that it's supposed to feel like one system, even if technically it's a lot of different systems working together," said Hansen.

One of ModUlf's biggest current hurdles is getting foreign residents to share their feedback.

People working on the programme try to conduct interviews and deploy feedback pop-ups, but many applicants are deeply hesitant to participate, Hansen explained.

This is often because people worry that complaining or pointing out problems could hurt their visa status, even though Hansen repeatedly said during the interview that they really need this feedback to better understand users' needs.

“It is difficult to get in touch with applicants. Specifically, for example, applicants who are in the process of appealing a case normally do not want to talk about their case with us. We haven't been able to get them to officially respond because not everyone wants to come to an interview," Hansen said. “For example, when we first made the new digital solution available for the police, we had researchers standing right there in the waiting rooms talking to applicants very informally, asking: 'How did you feel? What did you see? How did it go?' And a lot of people didn't really want to talk to us.”

“We do really want to talk to people, so we try quite hard to be able to do that," Hansen continued. "I don't think we have ever been quite so focused as we are now in talking with our applicants, because in general, our applicants and their experience with our system, is perhaps one of the biggest parts we focus now, because we see that there are quite a lot of complaints or that information is not available. How can we make this easier for our applicants?” wondered Hansen.

He stressed that these user researchers operate completely independently from case-processing personnel, meaning your feedback can never influence the outcome of a residency application.

"My main message is that they should not be scared. We're not going to use your feedback against anyone. The entire point is that we need your help to make good systems that affect applicants positively. So, if you get the opportunity or you receive an email asking for your opinion, please do help us. We really, really want those opinions, because it helps us immensely to adjust. If we don't get that insight, it's very difficult to build good systems for applicants,” said Hansen.

Currently, ModUlf does not have its own feedback portal. You can use the general "Feedback on service" form on UDI.no, which the digital teams check regularly. And, if you are ever approached in person by a researcher at a police station, giving them just five minutes of your time can make a massive difference.

The development teams also closely monitor trends within the UDI telephone support service to pinpoint exactly where applicants are getting confused by the language or user interfaces.

“We also pay close attention to how many people are calling into our telephone service to ask questions. We look closely at the data. Have we got more people calling in now because they don't understand something? Are we getting fewer calls? What is the general content of those calls? Why are they calling us?" Hansen explained.

READ ALSO: 'I am powerless': How waiting for answers from Norway's UDI impacts lives

What does ModUlf mean for applicants in the long run?

The ModUlf project should mark a definitive "before and after" for an immigration system that has felt outdated, rigid, and unfair for far too long.

As many readers have shared with The Local in previous surveys, it often feels unbelievable that such bureaucratic hurdles still persist in 2026; so it is reassuring to see the government actively working to change this situation.

ModUlf should fundamentally redefine how foreign residents interact with the state and, above all, transform their relocation process into a much smoother experience.

By replacing Norway’s crumbling digital foundation, the state hopes to build an immigration infrastructure that can offer predictable timelines, greater transparency, and real-time application tracking.

This change will also mean less need to contact staff, fewer back-and-forth conversations, and fewer frustrating moments where it feels like your outcome depends on which official you get.

Ultimately, international residents hope for much shorter waiting times.

From a human perspective, many applicants simply want to feel that they are not just another anonymous number in a machine, but that they are seen, valued, and that their cases are genuinely being considered.

While technology alone cannot resolve broader geopolitical migration pressures or changing laws, this six-year overhaul is a critical step toward a system that treats applicants openly and fairly, offering reliable and accessible service even during busy times.

Do you think ModUlf will actually make a difference for applicants?

articles.title: REVEALED: How Americans spend their money differently to Europeans
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        How do households in Europe and the United States spend their money? Official statistics reveal key and perhaps surprising differences when it comes to food and housing.

Official statistics show that the biggest expenditure item across the European Union is food, while in the United States it is housing. In Europe, leisure also accounts for more than in the USA.

In EU countries, almost half (46 percent) of households’ budget in 2025 was spent on food (16 percent), housing, water and energy (15 percent), and transport (15 percent), according to the EU statistical office, Eurostat.

In the United States, instead, half of the households’ budget in 2024 was allocated to housing (33 percent) and transport (17 percent), while food accounted for 13 percent, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Doris Speer, a lawyer from New York and roots in Michigan, who has lived in France for more than 22 years, told The Local: “I am not surprised that housing takes a bigger portion of the budget in the US. For example, when you look at rental housing, landlords in many US cities have less restrictions on how much they can increase rent compared to many European cities.”

“But I am a bit surprised that the proportion spent on food is higher in Europe, because food prices seem to be lower here. This may have to do with differing inflation and the fact that fast food, which is cheaper, is more prevalent in the United States, while a lot of people in Europe tend more to cook at home or go to restaurants,” she added.

Speer is president of the Association of Americans Resident Overseas (AARO), a volunteer organisation founded in France in 1973 to advocate for the rights of Americans abroad as regards citizenship, voting, banking, financial reporting, taxation and social security/Medicare.

“Many cities in Europe have mass transportation systems, which exist only in few cities in the US. It is inexpensive to go around without needing a car. On the flip side, fuel cost is higher in Europe, although gas prices in the United States have also increased in the past year,” she explained.

Leisure is another area that takes a bigger proportion of the household budget in Europe.

Restaurant and accommodation services accounted for 10 percent of the expenditure, and another 8 percent was dedicated to recreation, sport and culture last year, according to Eurostat.

In comparison, in the US, 8 percent of the budget is allocated to ‘entertainment’.

“Overall, in Europe there is a stronger focus on social activities and more leisure time”, Speer continued. “By law, people work less hours – although they don’t work less – and have more holidays and social time.

In the US, when you take a new job, you are lucky to have two weeks vacations per year,” she added.

articles.title: Why cross-border shopping in Sweden just got cheaper for Norway residents
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The Norwegian krone has gained 14.5 percent in value against the Swedish krona since the start of the year. This difference means you can now save more on groceries, fuel, and everyday services when shopping in Sweden.

It is not a secret that cross-border shopping in Sweden (known as harryhandel in Norwegian)  is a popular way for residents in Norway to stretch their household budgets.

Among the most popular purchases are groceries and treats, ranging from protein and quality cuts of meat to soft drinks, along with fuel, alcohol, and everyday services.

Given current currency fluctuations, using Norwegian kroner now holds a clear advantage.

The Norwegian krone has become the best-performing G10 currency (the ten most heavily traded major world currencies) so far this year, while the Swedish krona has fallen the most.

According to Bloomberg data reported by Norwegian financial outlet E24, residents in Norway now have around 14.5 percent more purchasing power in Sweden than they did at the start of the year.

Back in January, 100 Swedish kronor cost about 110 Norwegian kroner. Now, the same 100 kronor costs only around 96 kroner.

This change means your money now stretches much further on everything you buy in Sweden.

For example, if you bought groceries worth 2,500 Swedish kronor in January, you would have paid 2,750 kroner. Now, the same groceries cost about 2,400 kroner, saving you almost 350 kroner on a single supermarket run.

On top of the currency savings, Sweden’s prices are already lower. So, 2,500 kronor buys you much more in Sweden than the same amount would in Norway.

The same logic applies if you cross the border to fill up your fuel tank.

READ ALSO: How much can you expect to pay for fuel in Norway?

Economists say this difference is due to Norway’s strong energy revenues (boosted by high energy prices and global instability), as well as big differences in interest rates set by the two countries.

Norges Bank’s policy rate currently sits at 4.25 percent, compared to Sweden’s Riksbanken at 1.75 percent.

Higher interest rates usually make a currency more attractive to international investors looking for better returns. This increases global demand for the Norwegian krone.

"One of the reasons why there has been such a big difference in how central banks have set interest rates is that the Swedish economy has performed much worse than the Norwegian one," Olav Chen, senior portfolio manager and head of allocation at Storebrand Asset Management, told E24.

Nevertheless, while a stronger krone benefits cross-border shoppers, it also means that policy rates remain high. As a result, Norwegian homeowners are still burdened with higher monthly mortgage repayments.

Ultimately, whether cross-border shopping makes financial sense depends on how close you live to the border, what you plan to buy, and whether you are purchasing in sufficient volume to ensure the overall savings outweigh travel time and costs.

All eyes are now on Norges Bank as it prepares to deliver its next interest rate announcement on Thursday, September 24th.

articles.title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Friday
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The autumn holiday (høstferie) kicks off in 7 of Norway's 15 counties, the government pledges 240 million kroner to boost employment, and more news from Norway this Friday.

Traffic, train strikes, and winter tyres for Norway’s høstferie

After returning to school in August, families and students across Norway are getting ready for their first big break of the year: the autumn school holiday, or høstferie.

Depending on where you live, the break falls on either week 40 or week 41. From Monday, students in Oslo, Agder, Nordland, Akershus, Østfold, Buskerud, and Finnmark will have their week off, while the rest of the country will take their break the week after.

READ MORE: How Norway's autumn school holiday dates vary across the country

If you plan to drive, be ready for heavier traffic. Roads will likely be much busier from Friday afternoon through the weekend as many people leave the cities.

If you were hoping to travel by train, keep in mind that the ongoing driver strike is still causing major headaches.

Rail operator Vy has already announced cancellations through to Sunday. There will be 145 cancelled departures on Friday, 96 on Saturday, and 76 on Sunday. This will be a major inconvenience for many people who already had their holidays planned.

READ MORE: Which routes are impacted by Norway’s train strike?

For those staying in the cities, local public transport in holidaying counties will also run on reduced timetables throughout the week, so check your local transport planner.

If you are going to the mountains, it may be a good time to check your tyres. The Norwegian Automobile Federation (Norges Automobil-Forbund, NAF) warns that you should switch to winter tyres if you are heading into higher altitudes, as snow has already hit several mountain passes.

"If you are staying in the lowlands, leave the summer tyres on," said Nils Sødal, senior communications advisor at NAF, in a press release.

Norwegian government to spend 240 million kroner more on getting people into work

A budget leak to news agency NTB, ahead of the official state budget presentation on October 7th, revealed that the Norwegian government will set aside an extra 240 million kroner to help more people get jobs.

This plan is part of the Labour Party's goal to get 150,000 more people working by 2030.

According to figures from the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV), around 702,000 working-age individuals are currently outside the labour market in Norway, including 110,000 young people.

Minister of Employment and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng told NTB, "It is moving in the right direction, but the numbers on exclusion are consistently far too high. This is one of our biggest challenges, and also one of the government's top priorities."

The extra money will go to youth job programs, wage subsidies for health and care jobs, and more support for immigrant women and young jobseekers who face mental health or social challenges.

Oslo unveils proposed names for eight new consolidated districts

Earlier this year, Oslo City Council announced plans to consolidate the capital’s 15 districts into eight mega-districts from January 1st, 2028.

Following an open public consultation held in the spring, city authorities have now unveiled their final proposal for the new administrative names.

The eight new districts would be called Vestre Aker, Gamle Aker, Gamle Oslo, Frysja, Hovin, Øvre Groruddalen, Østensjø, and Nordstrand.

Health Councillor Oluf Ulseth defended the choices, saying that half of the names keep existing district names and the other half use historic designations. "We believe that the proposal both gives good names to each district and represents a whole," Ulseth told Norwegian media. "The names of the new districts should highlight the city's history, geography and identity, while supporting a clear and future-oriented district structure."

However, the names have faced quick criticism for ignoring public preferences from over 2,300 consultation responses. Many residents wanted to keep traditional district names like Frogner and Sagene, or just keep the district numbers.

The full Oslo City Council will discuss and vote on the final names by November 1st.

Norway to launch unified national strategy to combat hate speech

The Norwegian government plans to launch a national strategy to fight hate speech and online harassment. The goal is to make public debate safer.

Minister of Culture and Equality Lubna Jaffery said that separate plans for fighting racism, antisemitism, anti-Muslim hatred, and discrimination will be combined into one strategy, which will be presented in 2027

This proposal comes after recent studies showed that 40 percent of local politicians have faced threats or harassment, while nearly four in ten young people say they have received hostile comments after speaking out in public.

Jaffery warned that without stronger protections, "only the most hardened of us will choose to be in politics or in the public debate and participate as engaged citizens. And then you get a narrow group of people," as reported in Aftenposten.

Chinese EV sales surge in Norway despite scepticism

Chinese electric vehicle (EV) brands now make up a quarter of all new electric cars sold in Norway. This comes even as consumer scepticism surrounding data privacy and geopolitical concerns continues to climb.

According to a survey of nearly 15,000 EV owners conducted by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association (Norsk elbilforening), 31 percent of respondents are sceptical of Chinese-made cars for political reasons, up from 23 percent last year.

"New cars are practically running computers. When data security and privacy get more attention, it is natural that more consumers will be concerned about where the cars come from and how the data is handled," Secretary General Christina Bu told Aftenposten.

Despite these concerns, China has gone from almost no market share in Norway in 2019 to becoming the country's second-largest supplier of new electric cars in the first half of 2026.

The survey also showed that scepticism toward Tesla dropped sharply, from 43 percent last year to 24 percent this year. The association said this is because there has been less media focus on CEO Elon Musk's political comments.
